• A service can be public: tick it, give it a public name (dns.example.com) and a WAN port. Public services need a port; lint warns when one lives outside a DMZ zone and notes a public service without a name.
  • OPNsense "Sync port forwards" plans one destination NAT rule per public service (WAN address and port → the host's address and the service's port), in the category automation:labdex, keyed [nat:host/service]. Rules you made yourself are never touched. The WAN interface and destination are settings.
  • Technitium split horizon (setting, on by default): each public name becomes a zone on the internal server with the service's internal addresses, so inside the house the name resolves to the host and not to the WAN address. The zone is created as part of the plan. Public DNS stays with whoever hosts it; labdex doesn't touch it.
  • The policy page of an OPNsense instance has a Zones table: per zone, the labdex rules, other pass rules on its interfaces and access-check gaps. A zone with only labdex rules and no gaps is "managed by labdex". "Check access" logs those zones.

docs.title: Firewall rules from the zone matrix
docs.text:
• OPNsense "Sync policy rules" (plan/apply) turns every matrix cell into pass rules on the source zone's interfaces, between the zones' aliases, with port aliases or tcp/443-style ports. A service's allow from that the matrix doesn't already cover gets a rule of its own. All of them live in the category automation:labdex, keyed in the description; nothing else on the firewall is changed.
  • "Rules no policy explains" lists your own pass rules between zones that the matrix doesn't allow. It's on the instance's Firewall policy page.
  • The rules are re-planned after inventory and policy changes, and wait for approval.

docs.title: Zone policy
docs.text:
• New Policy page: a matrix of zones, rows where traffic comes from, columns where it goes. A cell holds ports (any, port aliases, tcp/22, udp/53, ranges) and a reason. Anything not listed is denied.
  • Everyone can read it; admins edit it. Changes are recorded in History (type zone_policy), emit policy.updated and are part of the YAML export and import (zone_policy).

docs.title: Routing discovery
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin for OPNsense with FRR (its diagnostics API) or Cisco IOS-XE (RESTCONF: the BGP operational model and the ietf-routing table). "Read routes and neighbours" lists BGP neighbours (matched to hosts), the routed prefixes that aren't an inventory network, and the inventory networks the router has no route for. Default and host routes are left out; prefixes that are fine without a network can be ignored.
  • A neighbour that drops out of Established sends plugin.routing.neighbour_down. A Routing page and a dashboard widget show it.

docs.title: UniFi Network
docs.text: • New built-in plugin using UniFi's integration API (an API key, UniFi Network 9 or newer). Clients go into Discovery with address, MAC and name; UniFi devices (switches, access points, gateways) that are in the inventory report online or offline as host status. A dashboard widget lists the devices.

docs.title: Tailscale and Headscale
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read devices" puts every tailnet device's addresses into Discovery, so unknown ones can be assigned to hosts (e.g. in a 100.64.0.0/10 network in your remote-access area). Devices that are hosts report online as status; offline counts as no data unless you choose "down".
  • Widgets: the tailnet on the dashboard; a host's device, addresses, OS and key expiry on its page.

docs.title: k3s / Kubernetes
docs.text: • New built-in plugin, read-only with a service account token. "Read nodes" matches nodes to hosts, reports Ready / NotReady as host status, and lists drift against the cluster's feature (hosts with the feature that aren't nodes, nodes without it), nodes that match no host, and mixed kubelet versions. A Cluster page, a dashboard widget and a node widget on the host page.

docs.title: Proxmox VE (read-only)
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin with a read-only API token (PVEAuditor). "Import guests" plans one host per VM or container labdex doesn't know: a guest named by the convention keeps its name; any other gets srv-vm-<name>-NN (ct for containers) with its Proxmox name as a fun name. It brings the node as "runs on", the MACs, the VLAN's network and the addresses from the guest agent (VMs) or the container. Guests that match an existing host by MAC, address or name are linked to it instead. Templates are skipped unless you want them. Applying records each import in History.
  • "Check drift" (hourly by default) compares every linked guest with its host: name, MACs, addresses, node, and running vs. the host's status, and lists guests not in the inventory. A host setting "Known differences" explains drift, which then doesn't count. A Proxmox page, a dashboard widget and a host widget show it.
  • labdex never changes anything in Proxmox; creating guests comes after 1.0.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
• New built-in module. "Check certificates" (twice a day by default) connects to every https service in the inventory (by its link, or its address) and to other endpoints you list (mail.example.net:993), reads the certificate even when it isn't trusted, and records who it's for, the issuer, the expiry and whether it verifies.
  • Warns at 21 days and calls it critical at 7 (both adjustable): a plugin.certificates.expiring notification once per certificate and level, a Certificates page, a dashboard widget (soonest first) and a host widget.
  • The dashboard's Hosts tile counts active hosts no monitoring plugin reports on.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin over Uptime Kuma's own (socket.io) API. "Sync monitors" plans one monitor per service with a link (or, optionally, a port check for every TCP service) on the hosts the instance applies to, and changes or removes the ones labdex made when services change (they're marked labdex:<host>/<service> in their description; your own monitors are left alone). It runs after host changes, as a plan that goes through approvals. New monitors get the notification ids you list and certificate-expiry notifications.
  • "Read status" reports each host (up if a monitor of it is up, down if all are down) and each service: the Services page and its status dots now prefer a monitor over Discovery and say where the status came from. Monitors labdex didn't make count for the host their URL or address points at.
  • Widgets: all monitors on the dashboard (down first), a host's monitors on its page.
  • Needs python-socketio (the uptimekuma extra; in the Docker image).

docs.title: Beszel
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read host status" reports each host whose Beszel system (matched by address or name) is up or down, with CPU, memory and disk.
  • "Add hosts as systems" plans a Beszel system for every host the instance applies to that the hub doesn't know yet (address from a host setting or the primary interface). "Install the agent" (a host action) runs Beszel's install script over Ansible with the hub key, or a universal token for agents that connect themselves.
  • Widgets: every system on the dashboard (down first); CPU, memory, disk, load, uptime and agent version on each host.

docs.title: Host status from monitoring
docs.text:
• Status plugins report what they know about hosts. A host's status: down if any source says down, up if at least one says up, otherwise what Discovery last saw. A report older than "Monitoring reports are fresh for … minutes" (General, 15 by default) counts as no data.
  • The host list has a status dot and a column per source; the sidebar tree and the dashboard use the same status; a host's Plugins tab lists each source with its detail and since when.
  • When an active host goes from up to down or back, a host.down / host.up notification goes out (Discovery alone never sends one).
  • For plugin authors: ctx.report_status({host: {"state", "detail", "data"}}) and ctx.match_host(), which maps an address, name, FQDN (any generated DNS name), URL or host:port to an inventory host.

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read host status" (every 2 minutes by default) asks the status query (up), matches each target's instance label to a host and reports it down when every target of the host is down. Basic or bearer authentication.
  • Widgets: "Targets down" on the dashboard; CPU over the last 6 hours (and memory) on each host, from node_exporter queries you can change.
  • Schedulable actions may set a default interval in the manifest (schedule_default).

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
• Plugins can show widgets on the dashboard and on a host's overview. They return data in fixed kinds (stat, status, list, table, sparkline) and labdex draws them: no plugin code runs in the browser, unknown kinds and fields are dropped and links must stay inside labdex or go to http(s). Results are cached per widget (refresh) and a slow or broken widget shows an error without holding up the page.
  • Host widgets appear only where the instance applies to the host, and only to people who can see both.
  • Built in: Backup → "Last backup" on the dashboard (age, kept, encrypted or not); nmap → "Open ports" on each host (documented or not).
  • API: GET /api/widgets, GET /api/hosts/<name>/widgets. Manifest: widgets: with id, label, where (dashboard, host), size (small, wide), refresh.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
• One Plugins section replaces Integrations. The sidebar's "Plugins" page shows every plugin with what it brings (actions, plans, exports, hooks, pages, host, endpoints, widgets, Ansible: read from its manifest) and its instances, filtered to the ones in use. Each plugin has its own page with its instances, actions, hooks and recent jobs; an instance (what used to be called an integration) keeps its page and settings. /integrations redirects; the API keeps its names.
  • GET /api/plugins/<id>; /api/plugins lists each plugin's instances and capabilities.

docs.title: Signed repositories
docs.text:
• Marketplace URLs are replaced by repositories: a signed index.json on any web server. The repository's key signs the index and every plugin in it. Adding one shows its name and key id first; the key is pinned, so a changed or re-signed index and plugins signed with another key are refused. Removing a repository stops the plugins only it vouched for. Indexes signed with the labdex project key show as official.
  • labdex plugin repo SOURCE OUTPUT --key KEY --name NAME signs every plugin folder, zips them and writes the signed index, ready to publish.
  • Unsigned marketplace URLs from 0.6 are no longer used; Admin → Plugins lists them.
  • API: /api/plugin-repos (/preview, then POST with the key id); /api/marketplace lists the repositories' plugins; install with {repository_id, id}.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
• A start page (/, "Dashboard" in the sidebar): hosts (up, down, planned), networks, services, lint and Discovery at a glance; plans waiting for approval (yours first) and approved plans waiting for their window; what's failing (the newest run of each action in the last week, until it succeeds again) and what's running; the last changes; scheduled templates and change windows coming up; hosts per zone; a warning when no worker runs jobs or notifications can't be delivered.
  • Everything on it follows your permissions. GET /api/dashboard.
  • Plugin widgets on the dashboard come with the plugin rework in 0.7.

docs.title: Ansible Vault and secrets in variables
docs.text:
• Feature and host variables can point at a global secret instead of holding it: admin_password: {$secret: grafana-admin}. The value is filled in only when labdex runs Ansible (in a private temporary folder) and never reaches the inventory, the YAML export, the API or History. Secret values are masked as ******** in job logs, --diff output included.
  • Ansible runner: "Ansible Vault password" (and an optional vault id) for files in your playbooks that are encrypted with ansible-vault.
  • File exports: with a vault password, the Ansible inventory export writes secrets as !vault values (Ansible's own format, 1.1 or 1.2 with a vault id), so a playbook run outside labdex decrypts them with the same password. Without one they stay references.
  • Lint: secret-missing when variables point at a secret that doesn't exist. The Secrets page lists features and hosts among "used by".
  • Secret settings of an integration no longer appear in labdex_settings.

docs.title: Job templates
docs.text:
• An action with its parameters (and host, for host actions) saved under a name, on the integration's page: run it with one click, or on a schedule (every N minutes, or on chosen days at a time in a time zone). Scheduled plans go through approvals like any other plan.
  • Running a template needs the right to apply the integration (and the host); a schedule, which runs unattended, needs admin rights on the integration. Jobs show the template they came from. API: /api/job-templates (+ /run).

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
• Channels (Admin → Notifications): ntfy (server, topic, optional token, priority), Matrix (homeserver, room id or alias, access token), email (SMTP with STARTTLS/SSL) and webhooks (JSON body; with a secret, an X-Labdex-Signature: sha256=… HMAC). Each picks its events and, optionally, which integrations it hears about.
  • Events: plan.waiting (needs approval), plan.applied, job.failed, backup.failed, host.down / host.up (for status integrations), test. Plugins send their own with ctx.notify(…), as plugin.<id>.<event>.
  • An outbox: messages go out from the worker, and failed ones are retried after 1, 5, 15 and 60 minutes. "Recently sent" lists them with the error; each channel shows its last message and how many failed. A Test button sends one right away and says what went wrong.
  • New setting "Address of this labdex" (General) for links back to the job.

docs.title: Approvals and change windows
docs.text:
• Approval policies (Admin → Approvals & windows). A plan is matched, top to bottom, by integration name, the zones of the hosts it runs for and how it was started (by someone, by a hook, on a schedule). The policy sets the approvals needed (0 = applies by itself), who may give them (users and @groups; empty = anyone who may apply the integration), whether whoever started the plan may approve it, a delay after planning, and a change window. Without a match it's as before: you approve your own plans.
  • Change windows: weekly times in a time zone (e.g. Tue and Thu 20:00–22:00 Europe/Berlin; a window may run past midnight). An approved plan waits as "approved" until its delay has passed and its window is open; the worker applies it.
  • A plan the inventory has moved past is planned again when it's approved or its window opens. If the new plan has the same changes, the approvals carry over; if not, it waits for approval again. A newer plan for the same action keeps the approvals of the one it replaces the same way.
  • The job page shows the policy, the approvals with comments, why you can't approve (not an approver, you started it, already approved), and when an approved plan applies. Approved plans can still be discarded, with a comment.
  • API: POST /api/jobs/<id>/approve {comment} (/apply does the same, for older clients), /discard {comment}; /api/approval-policies (with PUT …/order) and /api/change-windows. Approvals are recorded in History.
  • labdex action … --apply on the command line still applies right away.

docs.title: Worker and run history
docs.text:
• Jobs are a queue in the database. A dispatcher claims a job, runs it and sends heartbeats; a job whose worker stops (no heartbeat for 90 seconds) is marked failed instead of hanging in "running".
  • New labdex worker [--slots N]: runs queued jobs and the scheduler in its own process. With LABDEX_WORKER=external the web server only queues jobs (Ansible runs and scans stay out of the web process, and several gunicorn workers on PostgreSQL become possible). The default, inline, keeps everything in one container. docker-compose.yml has a commented worker service.
  • About shows who runs jobs, the workers seen in the last minute and how many jobs wait; a queued job says when no worker is there to pick it up. GET /api/jobs/queue.
  • Run history per host: a "Runs" tab lists the jobs that ran for the host (host actions and Ansible runs that included it), and follows renames. GET /api/jobs?host=NAME; jobs list their hosts and worker.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A service has a description, "listens on" (every address, the primary interface, one network, or one address) and, for web links, "link by name or address".
  • Discovery ("missing services") and the OPNsense firewall access check only look at the addresses a service listens on.
  • "Allow from" is picked from zones, areas, networks and aliases (/api/services/sources); sources labdex doesn't know are marked, and lint warns about them (allow-from-unknown).
  • The Services page is a launcher: cards grouped by zone with an Open button, status from Discovery (answering / not answering / not scanned), filters and a table view.

docs.title: IPv6 discovery
docs.text:
• OPNsense "Import ARP and NDP tables": IPv6 neighbours (diagnostics/interface/getNdp) with their MACs, next to ARP.
  • OPNsense "Import DHCP leases": Kea DHCPv6 address leases too (kea/leases6/search); delegated-prefix leases (IA_PD) are left out.
  • nmap: "Also scan known IPv6 addresses" (on by default). A /64 can't be swept, so it scans the IPv6 addresses of the inventory's hosts and those Discovery learned inside the chosen networks' IPv6 prefixes, with nmap -6, after the IPv4 sweep.
  • Link-local, multicast and loopback addresses never enter Discovery.

docs.title: Prefix delegation
docs.text:
• OPNsense: new action "Read delegated IPv6 prefixes" (schedulable). It reads the prefix each WAN interface received (interfaces/overview/interfaces_info, ifctl.prefix) and moves every delegated network prefix to its subnet: prefix ID N of size /L inside the delegation.
  • A change is recorded in the network's history ("delegated prefix A → B") and announced, so host GUA addresses (interface ID × prefix), AAAA records and N6/H6 aliases follow on the next sync.
  • Delegated prefixes that don't fit (prefix ID too large) or whose WAN interface reports nothing are listed in the job log and left alone.

docs.title: IPv6 host addresses
docs.text:
• Each interface has an IPv6 interface ID (::53, or eui64 from the MAC). It is used in every IPv6 prefix of the network, so adding a GUA prefix gives every host its GUA address at once. An explicit address stays valid and stands for the prefix it lies in; a per-prefix override wins over both.
  • One AAAA record per prefix; H6 aliases, Discovery, lint (duplicates), Ansible (ip6_all), Prometheus targets and the firewall access check use every address.
  • The host form shows the addresses an interface gets while you type, offers the next free interface ID, and has per-prefix overrides under "per prefix…".
  • Network usage lists the next free interface IDs of each IPv6 prefix.

docs.title: Networks: address families
docs.text:
• A network has any number of prefixes, IPv4 and IPv6 (e.g. a ULA and a GUA). Each has a mask from a list, an optional gateway and DHCP range, given as a full address or a suffix (254 → .254, ::1), and a description.
  • IPv6 prefixes can be marked "delegated": from a WAN interface with a prefix ID and length. Resolving the live prefix from OPNsense comes in 0.5.7.
  • Overlaps inside a network and with other networks are refused.
  • Firewall network aliases (N4/N6) hold every prefix of their family; host addresses may sit in any prefix; Discovery, nmap targets and the firewall access check use all of them.
  • The Usage tab shows every prefix: addresses in use, DHCP pool, next free (IPv4).
  • The old single-prefix fields stay in the API and mirror the first prefix of each family. YAML stays short for simple networks and lists prefixes otherwise.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Firewall access check: only inbound rules can grant access. OPNsense lists its built-in "let out anything from firewall host itself" with direction out and no source or destination, which labdex read as any → any. Outbound rules still show in the host's rule list, marked "out".

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: • The network page has tabs: Overview (settings, aliases), Usage (addresses in use, next free) and Hosts (every host with an interface there, its addresses and MACs, and whether its home zone differs).

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: • The rest of v0.5 is split into small releases: address families (0.5.5), IPv6 host addresses (0.5.6), prefix delegation (0.5.7), IPv6 discovery (0.5.8), services (0.5.9). Dashboard, plugins rework, widgets and routing discovery are placed in v0.6 to v0.8.

docs.title: DNS zones
docs.text:
• A network can have a DNS zone of its own: empty = <host>.<network>.<domain> as before, @ = <host>.<domain>, or e.g. home.lab = <host>.home.lab.
  • A host can have a main DNS zone for its short name, fun names, service names and extra records (default: the domain). Address records follow their network.
  • Two networks in the same zone give a host distinct names (<host>-<network>); with @, the short name is the address record itself (no CNAME beside it).
  • The BIND export writes one $ORIGIN block per zone; conflicts are checked by full name.

docs.title: Service records
docs.text: • DNS-SD (_service._proto SRV + TXT) is now a checkbox per service, off for new services. Services from before 0.5.3 keep theirs.

docs.title: Technitium
docs.text:
• Syncs every zone labdex writes into. Each record goes into the closest zone that exists on the server; names without a zone there are listed in the job log.
  • "Extra zones to read" for import and the host panel (never written). The old single "Zone" setting still works and is read like an extra zone.
  • Works without permission to list zones (falls back to labdex's own zones).

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• MACs: nmap records them when it runs as root on the segment; after every scan the scanning machine's ARP table fills in the rest; ARP and Kea leases keep doing it too. Each MAC remembers where it came from.
  • New "MACs" tab: interfaces in the inventory without a MAC whose address was seen with one, filled in with one click (one history entry per host). VIPs are left out.
  • Open ports show the address's MAC and vendor.

docs.title: Sidebar
docs.text: • Only the zone tree scrolls, with its scrollbar space reserved: opening and closing zones no longer changes the sidebar's width.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Zones and Naming have their own sidebar entries (out of Admin); everyone can look, administrators change them. Features is always in the sidebar.
  • The role part of a hostname (srv-vm-<role>-01) is free text. The builder suggests defined roles and those already in use; defining one only adds a label.
  • The host field "role" is now function ("DNS resolver"), to stop the clash with the hostname's role. Older YAML files and API clients that send role still work; Ansible gets labdex_function (labdex_role stays until 0.7).
  • Fun name pools: four neutral built-ins (Greek gods, stars, trees, minerals) plus your own (paste a list). A pool can apply to categories, areas or zones; "Suggest" on the host form offers unused names from the matching pool.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
• Each host has a DNS tab: extra records (alias CNAME, A/AAAA, TXT, SRV, MX) with placeholders ({target}, {fqdn}, {ip4}, {ip6}, {host}, {fun}), and a switch per fun name to publish it or not.
  • An alias with an empty value points at the primary record, so it follows when the primary interface changes.
  • These records are part of the inventory (YAML, exports, Technitium sync). The Technitium module's per-host "extra records" moved here on upgrade.

docs.title: About
docs.text: • About page (user menu, Admin → General): version, schema, database, plugins with versions and trust, and this changelog. Optional check for new releases on GitHub (off by default; Admin → General).

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
• A host's home zone now follows its primary interface's network (or the first interface in a network). Choose "pin" to keep a zone of your own. When a network changes zone, hosts that follow it move along, with a history entry.
  • Zone is picked as area + trust level. New hosts no longer default to a zone that may not exist.
  • Every address shows its network's zone. Someone who may see a zone can now view (not edit) hosts with an address there, e.g. the edge firewall for a DMZ-only user. The sidebar puts such hosts in the zone they can see.
  • Upgrading pins exactly the hosts whose zone differed from their network.

docs.title: VIPs
docs.text:
• New host kind "VIP": a shared address with a protocol (CARP, VRRP, keepalived, kube-vip, MetalLB, anycast) and member hosts. It gets DNS, firewall aliases and services like any host. Members list it on their Network tab and get labdex_vips plus a vip_<name> group in Ansible. The VIP itself is never an Ansible target and has no MAC. Hostname type vip added.
  • Member renames and deletions are followed; YAML import/export keeps members.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Host pickers (Discovery "add to host…", VIP members) are no longer cut off by the table; full names, keyboard selection, flips upwards near the bottom.
  • Migrations on SQLite run with foreign keys off, so rebuilding a table can't cascade-delete interfaces.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• OPNsense and Technitium calls checked against the sources of OPNsense 26.1 (Kea inside OPNsense) and Technitium DNS Server 15.6.2; contract tests pin them.
  • OPNsense grid searches POST rowCount: -1 (all rows) and fall back to GET.
  • Firewall rules are recognised as labdex's by the UUID of the automation:labdex category, which is what OPNsense returns.
  • Technitium: the API token goes in Authorization: Bearer, not the form body; the host panel matches every fun name of a host.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
• UI query cache (stale-while-revalidate): pages show the last answer at once and refresh in the background; every change, from any tab or the CLI, arrives on the event stream (revision) and refreshes what's on screen.
  • List pages stay alive: back from a host keeps filters, search and rows.
  • Host links prefetch on hover; saving a host writes the answer into the cache.
  • The host picker loads four fields instead of whole hosts.
  • Host list renders 200 rows at a time; search no longer matches field names.
  • Server: weak ETags with 304 Not Modified on every GET; a per-revision host index behind the host list, sidebar and counts (1000 hosts: host list 45 ms, sidebar 60 ms, slim list 5 ms).
  • /api/hosts: fields, q, zone, status, sort, limit/offset (X-Total-Count); cursor paging on history and jobs (X-Next-Before).
  • Static files: hashed assets cached for a year, precompressed .br/.gz.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
• Alembic migrations, run on start; a 0.4 database is adopted automatically.
  • PostgreSQL support (optional; SQLite stays the default). The test suite runs on both.
  • labdex db current | upgrade | copy --to URL (move SQLite → PostgreSQL).
  • Backups carry a portable database.json and restore into either database.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
• GitHub Actions: tests on SQLite and PostgreSQL, browser tests (Playwright), a performance budget on 1000 generated hosts, Docker build; multi-arch images to GHCR on tags.
  • tools/big_inventory.py makes large test inventories.
  • Fixed: a hook-triggered re-run raised an error after starting the job.

Editable zones, discovery workflow (adopt, assign, paging, Kea leases and DNS records as sources), Server-Sent Events, sidebar with zone tree and module menu, plugin store with signatures and trust levels, host page tabs, dotted service DNS names, per-interface DNS, admin panel, Kea reservations, firewall aliases by id in automation:labdex, hostname builder, multiple fun names.
Module framework with selectors and per-host settings, Technitium DNS, OPNsense aliases and access checks, Ansible runner with features, secrets vault, backups (folder and S3).
Users, groups, roles and scopes, change history with revert, plugins with plan/apply, nmap discovery.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
An OpenAPI 3 description of every route is at /api/openapi.json (when signed in) and from labdex openapi -o labdex-api.json; point a client generator, Postman or Swagger UI at it. It is built from the routes themselves, so it lists exactly what the running version has. Request and response bodies are plain JSON objects there; the table below says what they hold.

JSON under /api; sign in with the session cookie (browser; writes also need the header X-Requested-With: labdex) or a bearer token. Validation errors come back as 422 with a list of {field, message}; missing permissions as 403; objects outside your scope as 404.

Every successful GET carries a weak ETag; send it back as If-None-Match and an unchanged answer is an empty 304. Lists page with a cursor: /api/history and /api/jobs take limit and before=<id> and return the next cursor in X-Next-Before. /api/hosts takes fields=name,zone,…, q=, zone=, status=, sort=name|-zone|ip|…, limit= and offset=, with the total in X-Total-Count.

Hosts, networks and zones carry a uid (ten characters, never changes); every path that takes a host or network name (/api/hosts/<name>, /api/networks/<name>, …) takes the uid as well, so scripts that keep ids survive renames.

Method Path GET /api/meta Zones, areas, settings, counts, your permissions GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/hosts · /api/hosts/<name> Hosts (filtered to what you may see; can_edit per row) GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/networks · /api/networks/<name> Networks; /next gives the next free address GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/dashboards · /api/dashboards/<uid> Dashboards: {name, shared, items: [{type, x, y, w, h, config}]}; shared ones need an administrator GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/racks · /api/racks/<name or uid> Racks with the hosts in them; PUT/DELETE /api/racks/<rack>/hosts/<host> {unit, height, face} places or takes out a host; POST /api/racks/<rack>/items, PUT/DELETE …/items/<id> {kind, label, description, unit, height, face} for panels GET · POST /api/vault · /api/vault/{init,unseal,seal,passphrase} The vault's state (initialized, sealed, reauth_needed); setting it up, unsealing, sealing, a new passphrase (administrators) GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/vault/entries?host=&q= · /api/vault/entries/<uid> Secrets by name: {path, host, description, fields: {name: value}}; values are never in these answers. In PUT, a field's value null keeps it, fields left out go POST /api/vault/entries/<uid>/reveal · /api/auth/confirm {field, version?} → {value}, needs secret:apply, written to History; a browser session confirms its password first ({password}, every 5 minutes, else 403 with field password) GET · POST · POST /api/cables/suggestions · /api/cables/suggestions/accept · /api/cables/suggestions/ignore Cables switches see: suggested, conflicts (with what's now on record), unknown neighbours; accept {keys, replace}, ignore {keys} GET /api/cables Every cable you may see both ends of, with label, length (metres), colour; and next_label GET, POST · PUT, DELETE /api/topology/views · /api/topology/views/<uid> Saved topology views: {name, config: {view, zone, hidden_nets, lonely, grid, camera: {zoom, x, y}}} GET /api/zones/zones/<code or uid> One zone: its networks, hosts at home there, policy cells from and to it GET, PUT · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/topology?view=physical\|l3 · /api/topology/layout, /api/topology/cables[/<id>] The pictures (hosts carry live: up, down or unknown; cables an lldp check {state: seen|other|unseen, sees, source, protocol} when switches report neighbours), their shared arrangement, cables drawn on the map (both ends may be one host, on different ports); PUT …/cables/<id> {medium, speed, notes} changes one GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/aliases[/<name>] Aliases, generated and custom GET /api/services, /api/lint Services, convention checks (accepted ones carry accepted: the reason) POST, DELETE /api/lint/accept Accept a finding {code, kind, ref, reason} / count it again (administrators) GET · GET · POST /api/history · /api/history/<id> · /api/history/<id>/revert Audit log with diffs GET, POST · PUT, DELETE /api/searches · /api/searches/<uid> Saved Hosts searches, yours and shared ones PATCH /api/hosts/<name> Change some fields (name, kind, site, zone, status, function, fun_names, tags, features, notes); dry_run: true returns the site-file YAML before and after GET /api/hosts/<name>/yaml The host as its site file lists it, and the git branch and path it goes to GET /api/workloads Every Compose stack of the compose integrations you may see GET, PUT /api/workloads/<integration>/<host>/<name> One stack with its compose file; PUT {compose, dry_run} changes it (integration admin) PUT /api/hosts/<name>/yaml Replace the host with its entry as YAML ({yaml, dry_run}); cables stay. A dry run answers the file's lines before and after POST /api/hosts/bulk One change to many hosts: status, runs on, tags, features, zone, integration, delete GET /api/hosts/<name>/label.svg · /api/cables/label.svg?host=&port= Printable labels with a QR code (size=62x29, 50x25, 89x36) POST /api/admin/import/external Add networks and hosts from NetBox, phpIPAM or CSV (apply: false previews) GET /api/history/changes?since=7d Net change per object since a point in time (24h, 2w, a date; until optional) GET /api/discovery/{summary,services,missing,unknown-hosts} Discovery GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/integrations · /api/integrations/<name> Integration instances POST /api/integrations/<name>/actions/<action> Start a job (202) GET /api/integrations/<name>/export/<action>, /endpoints/<id> Exports, plugin endpoints GET · POST /api/jobs[/<id>] · /api/jobs/<id>/{apply,discard} Jobs and plans GET · PUT /api/hosts/<name>/modules · /api/hosts/<name>/modules/<integration> Integrations for a host: on/off, host settings GET · POST …/modules/<integration>/view · …/actions/<action> Host panel, host actions GET, POST · PUT, DELETE /api/features · /api/features/<path> Feature tree GET · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/zones · /api/zones/{areas,trust}[/<code>] Areas and trust levels; POST /api/zones/example GET · GET · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/naming · /api/naming/next?category=&type=&role= · /api/naming/<kind>[/<code>] Hostname parts, next free name GET, POST · PUT, DELETE · GET /api/naming/pools · /api/naming/pools/<name> · /api/naming/fun-suggest?category=&zone=&pool= Fun name pools, unused suggestions GET · POST /api/about · /api/about/update-check · /api/about/update Version, schema, database, plugins, changelog; check for a release now; the new-release bar (administrators) GET /api/nav Sidebar: zone tree with live status, which pages to show GET, PUT, DELETE /api/me/sidebar Your sidebar: pins [{to, kind, label, key}], hidden and order (page paths); only for you. from_default: the pages follow the default; DELETE goes back to it GET, PUT /api/admin/sidebar-default Default pages for everyone (hidden, order; administrators) GET /api/statusbar Status bar: per site the git commit (short), sync time, branch and file, linked agents of all you may see, vault state GET /api/events[?job=<id>] Server-Sent Events: plan count, revision on every change, job status and output POST · POST · DELETE /api/plugins/upload · /api/plugins/stage/<token>/confirm · /api/plugins/<id> Install, confirm, remove GET · POST /api/plugin-repos (/preview) Signed repositories GET /api/marketplace (?offline=1 skips the repositories) Everything installable: what repositories offer (installed, update, repo_version), and development checkouts (bundled) POST /api/marketplace/install {repository_id, id} Stages a repository plugin for /api/plugins/stage/<token>/confirm (a development checkout, {id}, installs at once) DELETE /api/plugins/<id> Uninstall (409 while it has instances) POST /api/plugins/restore Install the plugins this labdex uses but doesn't have (after an upgrade from 1.24.0) from the official repository now: {installed, failed, missing}; GET /api/plugins lists them as missing POST · DELETE /api/discovery/addresses/assign · /api/discovery/addresses/<ip> Add a seen address to a host; forget it GET · PUT, DELETE /api/secrets · /api/secrets/<name> The older API for vault entries under global/ (field value); writing needs the vault unsealed GET /api/vault/refs The fields you may point plugins and Ansible variables at: vault:<path>#<field> GET /api/dashboard, /api/widgets, /api/hosts/<name>/widgets Start page, widgets GET · PUT /api/zone-policy Zone matrix (PUT one cell: {src, dst, ports, description}; admins) POST /api/jobs/<id>/approve, /api/jobs/<id>/discard {comment} GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/approval-policies, /api/change-windows Approvals and windows (PUT /api/approval-policies/order) GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/notification-channels (/<id>/test), /api/notifications Notifications GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/job-templates (/<id>/run) Job templates GET /api/plugins/<id>, /api/jobs/queue Plugin details, the job queue /api/auth/*, /api/admin/* Sign-in, tokens; users, groups, roles, bindings, grants, backup/restore

Within 1.x, fields and endpoints are added, not removed or renamed (Upgrading).

docs.title: Change sets
docs.text: GET/POST /api/changesets, GET/PUT/DELETE /api/changesets/<uid>, POST /api/changesets/<uid>/preview and /apply (422 with the report when a change is refused). A body is {name, description, yaml}.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
labdex import inventory.yaml       # replace the inventory (asks first; --yes to skip)
labdex export -o inventory.yaml    # write the inventory
labdex sites                       # the sites with their networks, hosts and integrations
labdex export --site public -o labdex/public.yaml   # one site's networks and hosts
labdex import labdex/public.yaml   # a site file (top-level site:) replaces only that site
labdex lint                        # exit 1 on errors; --warnings-as-errors for strict CI
labdex plan FILE [--base FILE]     # what importing FILE would change; --format markdown for a merge request
labdex import-from netbox|phpipam|csv --zone DC_TC   # add from another tool; preview first, --apply keeps it
labdex changeset FILE [--apply]    # preview (or apply) a file of changes as one unit
labdex openapi -o api.json        # the OpenAPI description of the REST API
labdex diff --since 7d             # what changed since then (24h, 2w or a date; --fields for before/after)
labdex user create NAME [--admin]  # labdex user password NAME
labdex token create USER NAME [--read-only] [--days 90]
labdex plugins                     # plugins and integrations
labdex action fw-main sync_aliases [--apply]
labdex worker [--slots N]          # run jobs (LABDEX_WORKER=external)
labdex backup create -o FILE | check FILE | restore FILE [--inventory-only]
labdex db current | upgrade | copy --to URL
labdex plugin keygen | sign | pack | repo

Every command reads the same environment as the server (LABDEX_DATA, LABDEX_DB).

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Issues, pull requests and the licence of contributions: see CONTRIBUTING.md. Security problems: SECURITY.md, never in a public issue. How branches, versions and releases work: Branches, versions and releases.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
cd backend && pip install -e ".[server,postgres,uptimekuma,test]" ruff
pytest -q                                                       # SQLite
LABDEX_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://u@localhost/t pytest -q   # the same suite on PostgreSQL
LABDEX_E2E=1 pytest -q tests/e2e                                # browser tests (build the UI, playwright install chromium)
LABDEX_PERF=1 pytest -q -s tests/test_perf.py                   # performance budget, 1000 hosts
ruff check labdex tools tests                                   # pyflakes, pycodestyle, bugbear, pyupgrade
cd ../frontend && npm run lint                                  # ESLint: JavaScript and Vue rules (eslint.config.js)
cd ../frontend && npm ci && npm run dev                         # Vite on :5173, proxies /api to labdex run --debug
pip install mkdocs-material && mkdocs serve                     # these docs

Plugins for other systems are tested against small fake servers (tests/fakes.py) that follow the real API; tests/test_contracts.py pins the details that matter.

Official plugins live in their own repositories (labdex-plugin-<id>) and must have a labdex range, tests, and use nothing outside the plugin API. They aren't part of labdex and don't go into its image: plugins/ holds them as git submodules for development and the tests only (git clone --recurse-submodules). The tests load them through LABDEX_DEV_PLUGINS=plugins (set by tests/conftest.py); set it yourself to run a development server with them.

docs.title: Plugin API reference
docs.text: This is the stable plugin API of labdex 1.x: within a major version it only grows. Anything not listed here (other modules, models, private methods) may change.

docs.title: plugin.yaml

docs.title: Isolated plugins
docs.text:
Community and unsigned plugins run in a separate, locked-down process (see Installing plugins). For them:

  • self.ctx offers exactly the Context below; labdex's other modules aren't reachable (importing labdex.store works, but it has no database to talk to).
  • data_dir is the instance's own folder, kept between runs; the working directory and TMPDIR are a fresh temporary folder per call.
  • Everything you pass to labdex or return goes over JSON: keep return values to dicts, lists, strings, numbers, Change and ExportFile.
  • print() ends up in the job log.
  • Each call is a fresh process: keep state in set_state, not in module globals.
  • Calls time out after an hour (actions) or a minute (pages, widgets, endpoints).

Write plugins that only use this page, and they run the same either way.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin is a folder with plugin.yaml and, optionally, plugin.py and Ansible playbooks. Drop it into /data/plugins/<id>/ and restart (or Plugins → Reload).

# plugin.yaml
id: pihole
name: Pi-hole
kind: integration            # or module (exists once, no instances to add)
version: "0.1"
labdex: ">=1.0,<2"           # the labdex versions it works with (PEP 440 range)
description: Local DNS records in Pi-hole
applies_to: ["tag:pihole"]   # what a new instance applies to (default *); RBAC scope syntax
settings:
  - {key: url, label: URL, type: string, required: true}
  - {key: password, type: secret, required: true}
  - {key: networks, type: networks}          # string secret bool int select text list networks table yaml
  - {key: auth, type: select, default: token, options: [{value: token, label: API token}, {value: password, label: Password}]}
  - {key: token, type: secret, required: true, when: {auth: token}}   # only shown (and required) for that choice
host_settings:                               # per host, shown on the host page
  - {key: records, type: table, columns: [{key: name}, {key: value, required: true}]}
host_view: true                              # host_view(host) fills a panel on the host page
tags: [dns]
provides: [discovery]                        # shows the Discovery page (or: features)
pages:                                       # tabs on the integration, filled by page_<id>(args)
  - {id: overview, label: Pi-hole}
actions:
  - {id: test, label: Test connection, mode: run}
  - {id: sync, label: Sync records, mode: plan, schedulable: true}
  - {id: hosts_file, label: hosts file, mode: export}
  - {id: deploy, mode: plan, ansible: playbooks/deploy.yml}   # Ansible: check+diff, then apply
  - {id: restart, mode: run, scope: host, danger: true,       # per host, with a form for parameters
     params: [{key: service, type: string, required: true}]}
hooks:
  - {events: ["host.*", "network.*"], action: sync}
endpoints:
  - {id: targets, label: JSON for something to poll}
widgets:
  - {id: queries, label: DNS queries, where: dashboard, size: wide, refresh: 60}

# plugin.py
from labdex.plugins.base import Change, ExportFile, Plugin as Base, PluginError

class Plugin(Base):
    def run_test(self, params):
        self.ctx.http(self.settings["url"]).get("api/info")
        return {"message": "ok"}

    def plan_sync(self, params):           # a list of Change
        want = {r["fqdn"]: r for r in self.ctx.inventory.dns_records() if r["type"] == "A"}
        return [Change("create", "record", fqdn, f"A {r['value']}", after=r, data=r) for fqdn, r in want.items()]

    def apply_sync(self, changes, params):  # the reviewed plan
        for c in changes:
            self.log(f"creating {c.name}")
        return {"applied": len(changes)}

    def export_hosts_file(self, params):
        return ExportFile("hosts.txt", "text/plain", "...")

    def endpoint_targets(self, params):
        return [...]

    def host_view(self, host):
        return {"summary": [{"label": "records", "value": 3, "tone": "ok"}],
                "sections": [{"title": "Records", "type": "table", "columns": [{"key": "name", "label": "Name"}],
                              "rows": [{"name": "nas", "_tone": "warn"}]}]}

    def widget_queries(self, host):         # host is None on the dashboard
        return {"kind": "sparkline", "points": [1, 3, 2], "unit": "q/s"}

Methods are found by name: run_<action>, plan_<action> and apply_<action>, export_<action>, endpoint_<id>, page_<id>, widget_<id>, host_view. Raise PluginError("…") for errors the user should read. The reference lists everything a plugin can use.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
labdex.testing tests a plugin without a running labdex. PluginHarness loads your plugin folder, checks the manifest the way labdex does at install, and calls the plugin with a real Context: the real inventory (from a YAML file, text or dict, in a throw-away database), state kept in memory, the log in h.logs, notifications in h.notifications. FakeServer is a small HTTP server on localhost for the API your plugin talks to; it records every request.

from labdex.testing import FakeServer, PluginHarness

def test_sync_adds_missing_records():
    with FakeServer() as api, PluginHarness("plugins/my-dns", settings={"url": api.url}, inventory="examples/homelab.yaml") as h:
        api.route("GET", "/records", json=[]).route("POST", "/records", status=201)
        changes = h.plan("sync")                  # plan_sync(params) → [Change, …]
        assert changes and changes[0].op == "create"
        h.apply("sync", changes)                  # apply_sync(changes, params)
        assert api.calls("POST", "/records")[0].json["name"] == changes[0].name

h.run(action), h.plan, h.apply, h.export, h.endpoint, h.page, h.widget and h.host_view(host) call the methods of the same names; host_settings={host: {…}} fills a host's module_settings. api.route(method, path, json=…, status=…, text=…, handler=fn) answers a request (a path ending in * matches everything below it), api.calls(method, path) lists what came in. Your plugin's code runs in the test process, not in the sandbox that isolates community plugins, so you test its logic; the sandbox's rules are labdex's own tests.

To try it in a running labdex, start labdex run --debug with LABDEX_PLUGIN_DIR pointing at your plugins folder. labdex's own tests use the same kind of fake servers (backend/tests/fakes.py).

docs.title: Sign and pack
docs.text:
labdex plugin keygen my.pem                      # my.pem (keep it secret) and my.pem.pub
labdex plugin sign ./pihole --key my.pem --signer "Your Name"
labdex plugin pack ./pihole -o pihole-0.1.zip

People trust your key under Plugins → Signing keys (paste my.pem.pub); then your plugin installs as community.

docs.title: A plugin in its own git repository
docs.text:
That's how labdex's own plugins live (labdex-plugin-<id>): the plugin at the root of a repository, released by publishing a GitHub release. Start one from a plugin folder:

python3 backend/tools/plugin_repo/make_plugin_repo.py ./pihole ../labdex-plugin-pihole --community

It adds a README from the manifest, a licence (MIT for your own plugins, change it as you like; AGPL-3.0 for official ones), a CHANGELOG and the release workflow. Set the repository secret LABDEX_SIGNING_KEY to your private key. Then each release is: bump version in plugin.yaml, add a ## <version> section to CHANGELOG.md, commit, then publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> (in the web UI, or gh release create v<version> --target main --notes ""). The workflow checks the tag against the manifest, signs exactly what's committed and attaches <id>-<version>.zip to the release with CHANGELOG.md; the release description gets that version's CHANGELOG section (below anything you wrote). Files listed in .releaseignore (one pattern per line, like .gitignore: tests/, *.log, docs/draft.md) stay out of the zip; so do the repository's own files (.git, .github, .gitignore). labdex plugin prune <copy> does that by hand.

docs.title: A Marketplace from plugin repositories
docs.text:
A Marketplace is a repository with a plugins.yaml:

name: My plugins
description: Plugins by me
plugins:
  - repo: me/labdex-plugin-pihole
    withdrawn: {"0.3": "loses the blocklists on restart"}

Add discover: [{owner: me, prefix: labdex-plugin-}] and every public repository of yours named like that is included too, so a new plugin repository shows up by itself.

labdex plugin build-index plugins.yaml site --key my.pem reads every listed repository's releases (with GITHUB_TOKEN set it can make more API calls), checks each archive's checksum and that it's signed with your key, and writes a signed site/index.json that points at the release assets. Every release is a version people can install, update to or go back to, with its notes; a withdrawn version stays installable on purpose but warns everyone who has it, and updates skip it. Publish site/ on GitHub Pages: the labdex-plugins repository is a ready-made example (it rebuilds every hour, when plugins.yaml changes, and on a plugin-released dispatch from a plugin's release workflow).

docs.title: A repository from plugin folders
docs.text:
Or put each plugin in its own folder and build a repository with the archives in it:

labdex plugin repo ./plugins ./public --key my.pem --name "My plugins" --description "…"

This signs every plugin, zips them and writes a signed public/index.json. Publish public/ on any web server (GitHub Pages works). People add the URL of index.json under Plugins → Repositories, compare the key id with the one you publish, and install from the marketplace. The key is pinned: changing it means people add the repository again.

Each index entry carries the plugin's labdex range, so the marketplace only offers plugins that work with the labdex looking at it. Building into a folder that already has an index keeps the older versions whose archives are still there, so people can go back to them; labdex plugin fetch-repo <url> <folder> --key my.pem downloads what's published first. A plugin folder's CHANGELOG.md (## <version> sections) gives each version its notes.

Withdraw a version (or undo it) and re-sign the index:

labdex plugin yank ./public pihole 0.3 --key my.pem --reason "loses the blocklists on restart"
labdex plugin yank ./public pihole 0.3 --key my.pem          # offered again

docs.title: The official Marketplace
docs.text: Every official plugin lives in its own repository (labdex-app/labdex-plugin-<id>); labdex has them as git submodules in plugins/ for its tests, but doesn't ship them: users install them from the Marketplace. labdex-plugins lists them; its index is signed with the project key and published at https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex-plugins/index.json, which labdex trusts out of the box. Contributions are welcome: see Contributing.

docs.title: labdex's own versions
docs.text:
labdex releases are MAJOR.MINOR.SUB; a hotfix of a release is MAJOR.MINOR.SUB-N:

Version What it is 1.9.0 a release 1.9.0-1, 1.9.0-2 its hotfixes: bug fixes only, they come after 1.9.0 1.9.1 a small release 1.10.0 the next release

A hotfix is what Python calls a post-release (1.9.0-1 is 1.9.0.post1), so plugin ranges like labdex: ">=1.9,<2" take hotfixes as you'd expect. The image of 1.9.0-1 is tagged 1.9.0-1, 1.9.0, 1.9, 1 and latest: a hotfix replaces its release.

To make one, python backend/tools/bump.py sub|minor|major|patch (or an exact version) writes the version everywhere and opens a changelog heading. Push that to main, then publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> on it (gh release create v1.23.0 --target main --notes ""): the release workflow builds and signs the image and the files and attaches them, with the changelog section as notes if you left them empty. It refuses a tag that doesn't match the code's version.

docs.title: Branches, versions and releases
docs.text:
labdex uses release branches: main is where the next version grows, a branch per minor version is where it's stabilised and later patched, and every release is a GitHub release on that branch.

main ──●──●──●──●──────●──●──●──●──────────●──●──▶  (next: 1.25)
          \                 \
           release/1.23      release/1.24 ──●──●──▶
            v1.23.0  v1.23.1   v1.24.0   v1.24.0-1

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
MAJOR.MINOR.SUB, plus -N for a hotfix:

Change Version Branch New features (a release) 1.24.0 release/1.24, cut from main Small additions, docs, CI, no migration 1.24.1 release/1.24 Bug fixes only 1.24.0-1, 1.24.0-2 release/1.24 Breaking changes (a database or API that older clients can't use) 2.0.0 release/2.0

A hotfix sorts after its release (Python calls 1.24.0-1 a post-release), so plugin ranges like labdex: ">=1.24,<2" include it. Its image takes the floating tags (1.24.0, 1.24, 1, latest): installs that follow 1.24 get the fix.

Plugins are versioned on their own (version in plugin.yaml, MAJOR.MINOR) and released from their own repositories; a plugin fix never waits for labdex.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Branch For Protected main the next minor version; always green yes: pull requests with green CI only release/X.Y X.Y.0 and everything after it (X.Y.1, X.Y.0-1 …) yes: pull requests only feature/<topic>, fix/<topic> one change; short-lived no dependabot/… dependency updates, weekly no

Every change reaches main and release/* through a pull request. Every push runs Lint (ruff, eslint, YAML). Pull requests run only what their change can affect (.github/ci-changes.py decides, the "What changed" job shows why):

Change Runs a version bump alone (bump.py) nothing but the docs build (CHANGELOG) backend code the tests that code affects (pytest-testmon) on SQLite, the performance budget …with database code (queries, models), or into release/* the same on PostgreSQL too backend tests only the tests that changed frontend, or the API it calls the UI build and the browser tests Dockerfile the image build docs, mkdocs.yml, CHANGELOG, README the docs build Python or JavaScript dependencies, migrations, the plugins, CI itself everything

Running CI by hand (Actions › CI › Run workflow) runs everything, and so does the Monday run on main, which also keeps testmon's record current for new pull requests. Branch protection requires two checks: Lint and CI passed (the last job, which waits for the others).

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
1. Cut the branch when main has what the release should have: git switch -c release/1.24 main, then python backend/tools/bump.py minor (writes 1.24.0 everywhere and opens its CHANGELOG heading), fill in the CHANGELOG, and open a pull request into release/1.24. Nothing new goes in from here on: fixes only.
  2. Plugins first. If the release needs new plugin versions, merge and release those in their repositories (they're then in the Marketplace) and point the submodules at them in the same pull request.
  3. Release. When CI is green and the pull request is merged, publish a GitHub release on release/1.24 tagged v1.24.0 (gh release create v1.24.0 --target release/1.24 --notes ""). The release workflow checks the tag against the code, builds the image on amd64 and arm64, signs everything, attaches the files and the CHANGELOG section, and publishes this version's docs.
  4. Back to main. Merge release/1.24 into main (a pull request), so the version, the CHANGELOG and any fixes made on the branch are there too. Then bump.py minor on main starts 1.25.0.

docs.title: Fixing a release
docs.text:
1. Branch from the release branch: git switch -c fix/<topic> release/1.24.
  2. Fix it, with a test. python backend/tools/bump.py patch (1.24.0 → 1.24.0-1) and a CHANGELOG entry.
  3. Pull request into release/1.24; once merged, publish v1.24.0-1 on release/1.24.
  4. Pull request release/1.24 → main (or cherry-pick the fix), so the next version has it.

Only the newest release branch gets hotfixes, unless a fix is about security: then the previous one too.

docs.title: What each release has
docs.text:
• a GitHub release with the CHANGELOG section, labdex's own source (not the plugins), the wheel, their SBOMs and cosign bundles
  • ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:<version> for amd64 and arm64, signed, with its SBOM attached, also as <X.Y>, <X> and latest (latest is always the newest release)
  • its own docs: https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex/<X.Y>/ (the version picker at the top); latest is the newest release, dev is main

Between releases, every push to main publishes ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:dev (the newest commit) and :sha-<7 hex> (that commit), signed, for amd64 and arm64. They are for testing: they never move latest or a version tag.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] CHANGELOG: what changed, for the people running it (not the commits)
  • [ ] Upgrading from the previous release works (tests/test_upgrade_gate.py and the migration tests)
  • [ ] Docs describe the new behaviour; screenshots are current (docs/screenshots.py)
  • [ ] New plugin versions are released and the submodules point at them
  • [ ] CI is green on the pull request

docs.title: A first agent, read-only
docs.text: Try the agent on one host before you roll it out. Use a VM that nothing depends on, and leave the writes off: the agent then only reads, and you can take it all back with one command.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The host: Debian 12 or newer, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, Fedora or RHEL 9, with systemd and Python 3.11 or newer (python3 --version). A VM or a container with systemd will do. Take a snapshot first if it is a VM.
  • labdex: reachable from the host over https://, with this host in the inventory. If its certificate is from your own CA, copy that CA's certificate to the host for --ca-file.
  • A reverse proxy in front of labdex must pass WebSockets through for /api/agents/link. For client certificates, set it up as in Client certificates first, or leave LABDEX_AGENT_MTLS at optional for the trial.
  • Outgoing only: the host opens one connection to labdex. Open no port on the host.

docs.title: Rehearse it first (optional)
docs.text:
With Docker on your computer and a labdex checkout, rehearse all of this in a throwaway container with systemd, against a local labdex that requires client certificates:

cd backend && pip install -e ".[server]" && python tools/agent_rehearsal.py

It installs read-only, checks the link, the certificate and the read-only jobs, revokes, and uninstalls. It ends with all 13 checks passed, or says what failed. It touches nothing outside the container and a temporary folder.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. In labdex, open the host, then the Agent tab, and choose Enrol an agent. Leave run it as root unticked. Copy the command; its token works once, for an hour.

  2. On the host, download install.sh and read it. Then run the command, without --allow and without --root:

    curl -fsSLo install.sh https://lantern.example.net/api/agents/install.sh
less install.sh
sudo sh install.sh --url https://lantern.example.net --token lxe_… --sha256 …

  3. It ends with labdex agent installed and running as labdex-agent.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
On the host:

systemctl status labdex-agent        # active (running)
labdex-agent health                  # "the hub answered … s ago"
sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/labdex-agent # only ss and docker/podman ps: no apt, no shutdown
journalctl -u labdex-agent -n 20

In labdex, on the host's Agent tab:

  • the agent is linked and runs as labdex-agent. Under the settings, every capability says host doesn't allow;
  • under certificate, it says used on this link (if your proxy passes certificates);
  • choose Ping, then Facts, then Discover services. Each one shows up under the jobs, and the discovery tables fill in. The ports also appear on the Discovery page (source agent);
  • after a minute, the metrics show CPU, memory and /;
  • History for the host lists the token, the enrolment and each job.

docs.title: What it changed on the host
docs.text:
/opt/labdex-agent/labdex-agent.pyz the agent /usr/local/bin/labdex-agent a two-line wrapper to run it /etc/labdex-agent/agent.conf the hub's URL, writes allowed (none) /etc/sudoers.d/labdex-agent the read-only sudo rules /etc/systemd/system/labdex-agent.service the service /var/lib/labdex-agent/ key, certificate, audit log, offline buffer (mode 0700) user and group labdex-agent no shell, no home

Packages are installed only if python3, its cryptography package or sudo were missing; the script says which.

docs.title: Take it back
docs.text:
sudo sh install.sh --uninstall --purge

This stops and removes all of the above. Then choose Revoke on the host's Agent tab, so the key and certificate are dead in labdex as well. Revoking first works too: the agent stops at once and stays stopped until you uninstall it.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text: You see Look at enrolment refused (403): unknown, used or expired enrolment token make a new token: each works once, for an hour the hub URL must be https:// the URL in the command; labdex needs HTTPS for agents the agent logs no link to … and keeps trying the reverse proxy: WebSockets for /api/agents/link the hub wants a valid client certificate the proxy doesn't pass the certificate, while LABDEX_AGENT_MTLS is required the service stopped with status 3 labdex refused the agent (revoked, or root not allowed); journalctl -u labdex-agent says which discovery notes the sudo rule for ss is missing sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/labdex-agent, and that the service has no NoNewPrivileges (see What runs with privileges)

docs.title: Host agents
docs.text:
The agent is a small service on a Linux host that keeps one outgoing connection to labdex. The host needs no open port. Over that connection the agent:

  • sends a heartbeat with metrics every half minute (CPU, load, memory, /, uptime, network bytes);
  • discovers services: listening ports and the process behind each one (PID, user, command line, parent), running systemd units and running Docker or Podman containers;
  • reports waiting updates and whether a reboot is needed (the Patches page);
  • runs jobs that labdex signs, from a fixed list. There is no way to send it a shell command.

Writes are off until you switch them on, one capability at a time, in two places: on the host (when you install the agent) and in labdex (an administrator). Until then the agent only reads.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
On the host's page, open the Agent tab and choose Enrol an agent. labdex shows a command with a one-time token that works for an hour. Run it on the host as root:

curl -fsSLo install.sh https://lantern.example.net/api/agents/install.sh
sudo sh install.sh --url https://lantern.example.net --token lxe_… --sha256 …

Read install.sh before you run it. It:

  1. installs Python 3 (3.11 or newer), its cryptography package and sudo from the distribution, but only what is missing. The agent brings its other libraries along, so nothing comes from PyPI;
  2. downloads the agent (/opt/labdex-agent/labdex-agent.pyz) from labdex and checks it against --sha256;
  3. creates the system user labdex-agent (no shell, no home);
  4. writes /etc/labdex-agent/agent.conf and the sudo rules in /etc/sudoers.d/labdex-agent (checked with visudo first);
  5. swaps the token for the host's own key (/var/lib/labdex-agent/credentials.json, mode 0600; labdex keeps only a hash of it) and a client certificate (client.pem, mode 0600, see below);
  6. installs and starts the systemd service labdex-agent.

Options:

--allow "patch reboot ansible" the writes this host accepts. Without it the agent is read-only. --root run the agent as root instead of labdex-agent. labdex must allow root for this host too: only an administrator can tick run it as root when making the token. Ansible needs it. --ca-file /path/ca.pem for a labdex with a certificate from your own CA. --uninstall stop and remove the agent again: its service, sudo rules, config and program. The key, certificate and audit log stay in /var/lib/labdex-agent; add --purge to remove them and the labdex-agent user too. Revoke the agent on the Agent tab as well.

Running it again installs the agent anew with a new token, and revokes the older one. Without curl on the host, it downloads with Python instead; fetch install.sh itself the same way:

python3 -c "import urllib.request as u; open('install.sh','wb').write(u.urlopen('https://lantern.example.net/api/agents/install.sh').read())"

The hub URL must be https://: the key travels over it.

docs.title: What runs with privileges
docs.text:
The agent runs as labdex-agent. Its sudo rules allow exactly these command lines and nothing else (see them with labdex-agent sudoers):

Command Why When ss -Htulpn which process listens on a port always (read-only) docker ps …, podman ps … running containers always (read-only) systemd-run … apt-get update, … apt-get dist-upgrade, … dnf upgrade install updates with patch shutdown -r +1 reboot after updates with reboot

The agent's user is never put in the docker group, because that is as good as root. Write jobs run through systemd-run, outside the agent's sandbox, one at a time, and show up in the journal as labdex-agent-patch or labdex-agent-ansible.

The service runs in a systemd sandbox: ProtectSystem=strict (the only folder it can write is /var/lib/labdex-agent), ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, ProtectControlGroups, a capability bounding set that holds only what sudo needs to become root and what ss needs to see a socket's process, and limits on memory and tasks (see backend/labdex/agent/dist/labdex-agent.service).

Some hardening is left off on purpose. With a user of its own, systemd turns on NoNewPrivileges by itself as soon as a service has any of PrivateDevices, ProtectKernelTunables, ProtectKernelModules, ProtectKernelLogs, ProtectClock, ProtectHostname, RestrictNamespaces, RestrictRealtime, RestrictAddressFamilies, LockPersonality, MemoryDenyWriteExecute or SystemCallArchitectures. Under NoNewPrivileges, sudo can't run, so every sudo rule above would fail. This was checked on Debian 12 with systemd 252.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Job Writes? What it does ping no answers, to test the link facts no OS, kernel, CPU, memory, disks discovery.services no listening ports with their processes, systemd units, containers patch.report no updates waiting, reboot needed patch.apply patch (and reboot to reboot) install the waiting updates, then report again ansible.run ansible, and a root agent run a playbook from the site's git repository on this host

Every job is signed with labdex's own key (<data>/agent-signing.key). The agent saved the public half when it enrolled. It runs a job only when all of these hold:

  • the signature is good;
  • the job is for this agent;
  • it hasn't expired (ten minutes);
  • it hasn't run before;
  • it is on the list above;
  • for a write, the capability is on in agent.conf.

A job that fails a check is refused, and the refusal goes back to labdex.

Discovery and update reports run on a schedule (every hour and every six hours by default, changeable on the Agent tab, 0 turns them off) and on demand. Discovered ports go to the Discovery page (source agent) for each of the host's addresses they listen on; ports that listen only on loopback stay on the host's Agent tab. Passwords, tokens and keys in command lines are masked before they leave the host (--password ***, DB_PASS=***, https://user:***@…).

Ansible runs never carry a playbook or a command. labdex packs the folder that holds the playbook from the site's git working copy at its current commit (a .tar.gz, at most 8 MB). It sends the agent the bundle's SHA-256, the commit, the playbook path and the variables, all signed. The agent fetches the bundle over the same connection and checks the hash. It unpacks the bundle with no absolute paths, no .. and no links, then runs ansible-playbook -i localhost, -c local through systemd-run. Tick check only for --check --diff.

docs.title: All agents
docs.text: Agents in the sidebar lists every host's agent: linked or not, when it was last seen, whether it runs as root, which writes are on at both ends, whether the link used its client certificate, and its latest CPU, memory and / use. The tiles filter the list, for example to agents that link without a certificate before you switch LABDEX_AGENT_MTLS to required.

docs.title: Revoke
docs.text: Revoke on the Agent tab stops the key at once: labdex closes the live connection within a second, and the agent stops and stays stopped (RestartPreventExitStatus=3). Enrolling a host again revokes its older agent.

docs.title: Client certificates
docs.text:
On top of its key, each agent has a client certificate for mutual TLS. labdex is a small certificate authority for its own agents and nothing else (<data>/agent-ca.key and agent-ca.pem). At enrolment the agent makes a key pair on the host and sends a certificate request with the token. labdex signs a certificate for a year, named after the agent, and keeps its SHA-256. The private key never leaves the host. On every link the agent presents the certificate in the TLS handshake, and labdex checks that it is from this CA, in date, for this agent and the one on record. Thirty days before it runs out, labdex asks the agent for a new one over the link. The old one keeps working until the agent links with the new one. Revoke makes the key and the certificate worthless at once, so there is no revocation list.

LABDEX_AGENT_MTLS decides how strict this is:

optional (default) agents get certificates; a certificate that is presented must be right, but a link without one still works required no link and no enrolment without a certificate. Switch to it once the Agent tab shows used on this link for your agents off keys only

optional doesn't protect against a stolen key: only required does. The Agent tab shows the certificate's expiry and whether the current link presented it.

The certificate has to reach labdex from whoever terminates TLS:

  • labdex itself, with gunicorn's own TLS: add --cert-reqs 1 --ca-certs /data/agent-ca.pem to its --certfile/--keyfile.
  • A reverse proxy: it asks for a client certificate, checks it against labdex's CA (/api/agents/ca.pem), and passes it on in a header. Name the header in LABDEX_AGENT_CERT_HEADER and put the proxy in LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES. The proxy must overwrite the header on every request, so a client can't set it. Enrolment comes without a certificate, so make it optional, not required, at the proxy.

Caddy

lantern.example.net {
    tls {
        client_auth {
            mode verify_if_given
            trust_pool file /etc/caddy/labdex-agent-ca.pem
        }
    }
    reverse_proxy labdex:8000 {
        header_up X-Client-Cert {http.request.tls.client.certificate_der_base64}
    }
}

nginx

ssl_client_certificate /etc/nginx/labdex-agent-ca.pem;
ssl_verify_client optional;
location / {
    proxy_set_header X-Client-Cert $ssl_client_escaped_cert;
    proxy_pass http://labdex:8000;
}

Traefik

tls:
  options:
    labdex-agents:
      clientAuth:
        caFiles: [/etc/traefik/labdex-agent-ca.pem]
        clientAuthType: VerifyClientCertIfGiven
http:
  middlewares:
    labdex-agent-cert:
      passTLSClientCert:
        pem: true   # sent as X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert

With Traefik, set LABDEX_AGENT_CERT_HEADER=X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert.

docs.title: Offline
docs.text: When labdex can't be reached, the agent retries with backoff up to a minute. Job results and heartbeats wait in /var/lib/labdex-agent/buffer (at most 64 MB and seven days) and go out, oldest first, when the connection is back. labdex ignores a result it already has. Jobs that waited more than ten minutes for an agent that wasn't connected expire.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: labdex records enrolment tokens, enrolments, revocations, settings changes, every job you start and its outcome in the history of the host (object type agent). Scheduled read-only runs are recorded only when they fail. The agent writes its own log, /var/lib/labdex-agent/audit.log: one JSON line for every job it accepted, refused or finished, without the job's output.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
GET /api/agents/metrics returns each connected agent's latest heartbeat in the Prometheus text format, as labdex_agent_* with host and agent labels. Point VictoriaMetrics at it with an API token. labdex itself keeps no history of these numbers.

The latest values also show in labdex while the agent is linked: CPU, memory and disk use (/) on the host page, as columns on the hosts list and in a host's Guests table, and as each site's average under Capacity in the Overview's Sites table. Hosts without a linked agent show a dash.

docs.title: On the host
docs.text:
systemctl status labdex-agent
labdex-agent health                 # exit 0 while labdex answered in the last two minutes
labdex-agent show discovery         # what discovery would report, printed here, nothing sent
labdex-agent sudoers                # the sudo rules for this host's capabilities

labdex-agent (in /usr/local/bin) runs /usr/bin/python3 -I /opt/labdex-agent/labdex-agent.pyz. Its log is in the journal: journalctl -u labdex-agent. Write jobs log there too, as labdex-agent-patch and labdex-agent-ansible.

docs.title: Running labdex for agents
docs.text:
Each connected agent holds one of the web server's threads. The image starts gunicorn with 64 threads. With many agents, raise --threads in the container's command. Behind a reverse proxy, pass WebSockets through for /api/agents/link.

The agent replaces labdex-patch-report, which still works for hosts without an agent.

docs.title: Change sets
docs.text:
A change set is a batch of inventory changes you review as one unit: "move the guests to a new VLAN" is two networks and six hosts, and you want to see what it does before any of it is saved.

Open Automation › Change sets, or keep the file in git and use the command line:

labdex changeset guest-vlan.yaml            # preview: nothing is kept
labdex changeset guest-vlan.yaml --apply    # all of it, or none

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
networks:
  - {name: guest2, vlan: 232, zone: CA_UT, prefix4: 10.10.232.0/24, gateway4: 10.10.232.254}
hosts:
  - name: cli-lt-ana-01
    zone: CA_UT
    interfaces: [{network: guest2, ip4: 10.10.232.5, primary: true}]
aliases:
  - {name: GUEST_TWO_HOSTS, type: host, members: [cli-lt-ana-01]}
delete:
  hosts: [old-vm-test-01]
  networks: [guest]
  aliases: []

An entry that exists is updated: only the keys you give change, so {name: nas, function: Backup} leaves everything else on nas alone. An entry that doesn't exist is created. Order doesn't matter: networks come first, then hosts, then aliases, and deletions run hosts, aliases, networks, so a set can retire a network together with the hosts on it.

docs.title: Preview, then apply
docs.text:
Preview applies the file inside a transaction and rolls it back. The report lists every change (and the fields that change on updates), the lint findings it adds or resolves, the firewall aliases that appear, vanish or change, and the DNS records added or removed.

Apply checks everything again, since the inventory may have changed since you previewed, and saves it only if every change passes. One refused change (an address outside its network, a network still in use, a zone you may not edit) saves nothing. Each changed object gets a History entry named after the set, so a bad set can be undone object by object from History. An applied set is kept as a record and can't be applied twice.

You need the right to edit each object a set touches; a set never gives you more access than editing the same things by hand.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Everything is set with environment variables; conventions (domain, alias length, categories, the DMZ area) are edited in the UI under Settings → Conventions.

Variable Default LABDEX_DATA ./data (/data in the image) Database, secret.key, plugins/, backups LABDEX_DB sqlite:///$LABDEX_DATA/labdex.db or postgresql://user:pw@host/db LABDEX_SECRET_KEY generated into $LABDEX_DATA/secret.key Signs sessions, encrypts secrets. Keep a copy apart from backups LABDEX_ADMIN_USER, LABDEX_ADMIN_PASSWORD Create this administrator on an empty database LABDEX_PLUGIN_DIR $LABDEX_DATA/plugins Installed plugins LABDEX_PLUGIN_SANDBOX on Community and unsigned plugins run isolated (see Installing plugins). strict: only where the kernel has Landlock; off: inside labdex like official plugins LABDEX_SSO_HEADER e.g. Remote-User, trusted only from LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES LABDEX_SSO_GROUPS_HEADER e.g. Remote-Groups, matched to labdex groups by name LABDEX_SSO_AUTOCREATE false Create users on their first SSO visit LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES Proxy addresses allowed to send SSO headers (and agents' client certificates) LABDEX_AGENT_MTLS optional Client certificates for host agents: off, optional or required LABDEX_AGENT_CERT_HEADER e.g. X-Client-Cert: the header a reverse proxy passes an agent's client certificate in, trusted only from LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES LABDEX_OIDC_ISSUER Sign in with OpenID Connect, see below LABDEX_COOKIE_SECURE false true behind HTTPS LABDEX_SESSION_HOURS 12 Session lifetime LABDEX_SCHEDULER true Run scheduled actions and templates LABDEX_WORKER inline external: only queue jobs for labdex worker LABDEX_DEMO false Demo mode. Wipes the database: never on a real instance LABDEX_DEV_PLUGINS Development only: a folder of plugin checkouts (the repository's plugins/) loaded as official plugins. Never on a real instance

docs.title: Single sign-on with OpenID Connect
docs.text:
labdex signs people in with Authentik, Keycloak, Authelia, Pocket ID, Zitadel or any other OpenID Connect provider (authorization code flow with PKCE). Create an application there with the redirect URI https://<labdex>/api/auth/oidc/callback (Settings › Users shows the exact one), then:
