docs.text: Running a workflow needs the right to apply on every integration its steps use (and on the host of a step for one host). Saving one with a schedule needs admin rights on those integrations, because it runs unattended. Each plan still needs its own approvals.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
GET/POST /api/workflows, GET/PUT/DELETE /api/workflows/<id> workflows (window by name or window_id) POST /api/workflows/<id>/run start a run GET /api/workflow-runs?status=open runs, newest first GET /api/workflow-runs/<id> a run with its steps: status, job_id, note, started_at, finished_at POST /api/workflow-runs/<id>/cancel cancel a run

A job that belongs to a run carries workflow: {run_id, name, step, of, status} in /api/jobs.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
labdex itself has no plugins installed apart from backups, which are part of it. Every other plugin, the official ones too, comes from Plugins › Marketplace: installing one downloads it from its repository and checks its signature first. Uninstalling one is refused while it has instances.

Upgrading from 1.24.0 or older, where the official plugins shipped inside labdex: labdex installs the ones you had from the official Marketplace by itself, right after the upgrade. If it can't reach the Marketplace, the Plugins page lists them (with an Install them now button); their instances keep their settings and history meanwhile.

The Marketplace also lists what your repositories offer, with a filter for updates. Anyone who can see integrations can browse it; administrators install.

Under Plugins add an instance of a plugin (an integration), fill in its settings and enable it. A plugin can have several instances, e.g. one per firewall. Each plugin has a page listing its instances, what it can do and its signature.

Plugin What it does OPNsense Aliases, rules from the zone matrix, port forwards, Kea reservations, access check, ARP and leases into Discovery Technitium DNS Records and split-horizon zones, plan/apply; stale and unmanaged records per host Ansible runner Features as playbooks and roles, --check --diff as the plan; host actions Login banner & prompt Banners and a zone-coloured prompt over Ansible nmap TCP connect scans of inventory networks into Discovery; every declared service port is checked too, whatever the port list VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus Host status from up, CPU and memory widgets Beszel Host status and resources; adds systems, installs agents Uptime Kuma A monitor per service; status read back Certificates TLS expiry of every https service Proxmox VE Imports guests as hosts, links, drift k3s / Kubernetes Nodes, readiness, versions, drift Tailscale / Headscale Tailnet devices into Discovery, online state NetBird Peers into Discovery, connected state, groups UniFi Network Clients into Discovery, devices as host status, cables from LLDP SNMP neighbours Cables from LLDP and CDP over SNMP v2c/v3 Traefik HTTP routers as services with their host names Docker Containers as hosts, published ports and Traefik labels as services, state as status Routing discovery BGP neighbours and routes vs. the inventory (FRR, IOS-XE) Prometheus service discovery http_sd_configs endpoints Backup Daily encrypted backups to a folder or S3 (Backups) YAML mirror The inventory as a file after every change, optionally in git File exports OPNsense alias import, DNS zone, Ansible inventory, DHCP CSV, YAML

docs.title: Applies to
docs.text: Integrations that work per host have selectors in the same syntax as role scopes. On a host's page each one shows whether it applies (and why), can be forced on or off, holds the host's own settings and actions, and shows a panel the plugin fills.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: API keys and tokens typed into a plugin's settings are encrypted at rest with a key derived from secret.key and are never sent back by the API. Shared ones live in the vault: pick from the vault on a secret setting and choose a field (vault:fw/opnsense#key); rotating it there updates every user. The list holds what you may reveal, since pointing at a secret hands it to the plugin.

docs.title: Widgets and status
docs.text: Plugins can show widgets on the dashboard and host pages, and report host and service status. A host is down if any monitoring source says so, up if one says up; without monitoring, Discovery's last scan decides.

docs.title: Ansible and features
docs.text:
Features are a tree (server → server.packages → server.packages.pve) with variables and playbooks or roles. Hosts get features; variables merge root to leaf, then the host's own variables. Making kube.cluster.oak makes kube and kube.cluster too when they don't exist yet (empty, ready for their own variables), in the UI, the API and a YAML import.

features:
  - {path: server, vars: {ntp: 10.10.3.253, pkgs: [vim, curl]}}
  - {path: server.packages, playbooks: [playbooks/packages.yml]}
  - {path: kube, vars: {version: v1.30.6}, roles: [k3s]}
  - {path: kube.cluster.oak, vars: {version: v1.31.2, vip: 10.10.128.10}}
hosts:
  - name: srv-vm-k3s-01
    features: [server.packages, kube.cluster.oak]
    vars: {k3s_role: server}

The Ansible runner applies features from a folder or a git repository: playbooks, then roles, ancestors first, each limited to the hosts that have the feature. --check --diff is the plan, the real run happens on apply. Per host it can apply the host's features, run a command or install packages.

Variables can point at a secret instead of holding it: {$secret: grafana-admin}. The value is filled in only while Ansible runs and is masked in logs. Files encrypted with ansible-vault work with the vault password setting; see Templates and Ansible Vault.

The same variables and feature_<path> groups are in the Ansible inventory export, so your own ansible-playbook runs see them too.

docs.title: Compose stacks
docs.text:
The Compose stacks integration keeps your Docker Compose stacks in labdex and writes them to the Docker hosts with Ansible. Like other plans in labdex, nothing reaches a host before a person approved the run, and labdex only ever changes folders it wrote itself.

Add it under Plugins › Compose stacks › Add. It lives in plugins/compose/ of the labdex repository for now.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• Ansible in labdex: build the image with docker build --build-arg ANSIBLE=1 .. Check setup says what's missing.
  • SSH to the Docker hosts: an SSH user and private key, and sudo for that user (the stack folder is created as root, docker compose runs as root).
  • Docker with the Compose plugin (docker compose) and Python 3 on the hosts.

docs.title: Stacks
docs.text:
Workloads (in the sidebar under Operate) lists every stack of every Compose integration you may see, with its host, services and last deploy. Pick one to read or change its compose file: Diff shows the change before Save, which changes labdex only (recorded in Activity as an update of the integration; comments in the Stacks text are not kept). Plan deploy plans that one stack, and the plan waits on Changes for an approval like any other.

Stacks is a YAML list. Each stack names the host it runs on, its compose file and, if it needs one, its environment:

- name: grafana
  host: srv-vm-docker-01
  compose:
    services:
      grafana:
        image: grafana/grafana:11.3.0
        ports: ["3000:3000"]
        environment:
          GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER: ${GF_ADMIN_USER}
          GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${GF_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
  env:
    GF_ADMIN_USER: admin
    GF_ADMIN_PASSWORD: {$secret: vault:apps/grafana#admin}
  • name is the compose project name and the folder: lower-case letters, digits, - and _.
  • host must be a host of the inventory that this integration applies to.
  • compose is the compose file itself, with at least one service.
  • env becomes the stack's .env file. A value is either written as is or is a reference to the vault, {$secret: vault:path#field}. Values are quoted so that compose takes them literally (a $ in a password stays a $).

On the host a stack becomes <folder for stacks>/<name>/ (/opt/stacks by default) with compose.yaml, .env (mode 0600) and .labdex, a marker with fingerprints of what labdex wrote. Show compose files prints the files without connecting to any host.

docs.title: Deploy stacks
docs.text:
Deploy stacks is a plan:

  1. Plan. labdex reads the stack folders on the hosts (read-only) and compares each compose file with the one in labdex, and the env by the fingerprint of its references. Secret values never leave the vault for a plan. The plan shows a diff of every compose file and says when the .env changed. A folder of the same name that labdex didn't write (no .labdex marker) stops the plan: rename the stack or move the folder.
  2. Approve. Every run waits for a person's approval, even when an approval policy would let it apply by itself.
  3. Apply. One play over the planned hosts: it writes the files, fills in the secrets for this run only (the .env task never shows up in the log), pulls the images if Pull images before starting is on, and runs docker compose up -d --remove-orphans.
Parameter Only these stacks stack names; empty = every stack

A stack you take out of labdex keeps running on its host. With Remove stacks taken out of labdex on, the plan includes it as a removal instead: docker compose down, then its folder is deleted. Only folders with the .labdex marker are ever removed, and volumes are kept.

Hosts in public sites

Approval policies decide who may approve which plan. Give the hosts of a public site a policy with the approvers you trust there; the plugin itself never deploys without an approval.

docs.title: Proxmox VE
docs.text:
A read-only API token (PVEAuditor) is enough for importing and drift. Import guests plans VMs and containers as hosts (names that don't follow your convention become srv-vm-<name>-NN with the guest name kept as fun name), links existing hosts, and reports drift (addresses, MACs, status) between the inventory and the cluster.

Check drift also hands the guests the inventory doesn't have to Discovery (turn Guests labdex doesn't know go into Discovery off to stop it): their addresses show up under unknown hosts as Proxmox VM 104 on pve1, with the guest name as host name and its MAC when it has one network card. Running guests count as seen; Add it as a host starts from there.

docs.title: Creating guests
docs.text:
Off until you turn on Create guests in the instance; the token then needs the PVEVMAdmin role plus Datastore.AllocateSpace on the storage and SDN.Use on the bridges. Then the inventory is where a guest starts:

  1. Add a host with status planned, an interface with its address in a network, and Runs on set to a Proxmox node (or set a default node in the instance). The type comes from the name (srv-ct-… is a container, srv-vm-… a VM) or from the host's Proxmox settings, where cores, memory, disk, storage and the template can be set per host too.
  2. Run Create planned guests (or Create this guest on the host). The plan shows each guest: node, template, size, bridge, VLAN tag and addresses. Nothing in Proxmox changes until the plan is approved.
  3. On apply, a container is made from the LXC template, a VM is cloned from the cloud-init template; the network comes from the inventory: the network's VLAN as the tag on the bridge (or the bridge per network you set), the static address with the network's gateway, IPv6 from the inventory or SLAAC, your SSH keys, DNS server and search domain. A MAC the inventory doesn't have yet is generated (Proxmox's BC:24:11 prefix) and written back, so DHCP reservations and drift line up.
  4. The host is linked to its guest and becomes active once started. If a later step fails (the VM doesn't start, say), the guest is still linked and the host set offline, so the next plan doesn't make a second one; the job log says what to fix.

Guests are never deleted; drift reports differences. Changing them is a separate switch each, below.

docs.title: Changing guests
docs.text:
Each kind of change has its own switch in the instance, all off by default, and each needs more privileges on the token (listed with the switch). Every run waits for a person's approval, even when an approval policy would let it apply by itself, and the plan lines carry the host, so zone policies apply (a public site can ask for its own approvers). They only touch guests linked to a host (VM / CT id in the host's Proxmox settings).

  • Start and stop guests: Apply guest settings starts a guest whose host is active in the inventory and shuts down (a clean ACPI shutdown) one whose host is offline. Planned hosts are left alone.
  • Change cores and memory: Apply guest settings sets cores and memory to what the host's Proxmox settings say; an empty field leaves the guest as it is. A VM's new memory takes effect at its next restart unless memory hotplug is on; the plan says so.
  • Take snapshots: Take a snapshot on a host snapshots its guest, with a name you give or labdex-<date>-<time>. With Snapshot before a change on (the default), Apply guest settings takes one before it resizes or shuts down a guest, so there is something to roll back to (rolling back stays in Proxmox).

Apply this guest's settings does the same for one host. A switch you turn off after planning still counts when the plan is applied: that part is skipped and the log says so.

docs.title: k3s
docs.text: A service account token with get/list on nodes and pods. Matches nodes to hosts, reports Ready/NotReady as host status, lists drift against the cluster's feature and mixed kubelet versions.

docs.title: Tailscale
docs.text: Tailscale or Headscale. Tailnet devices go into Discovery; devices that are hosts report online as status. Widgets for the tailnet and a host's device.

docs.title: NetBird
docs.text:
Peers of a NetBird network, on netbird.io or self-hosted, go into Discovery with their mesh addresses; peers that are hosts report connected or not as status, and the host page shows their groups, OS, version and an expired login. Read-only: it only lists peers.

You need a personal access token of a service user with the read-only role (Team › Service users). Self-hosted: set the management URL (https://netbird.example.net). Only peers in these groups limits it to, say, servers. A peer is matched to a host by its mesh address, its hostname, its name or the first label of its DNS name.

The plugin lives in plugins/netbird/ of the labdex repository until it gets a repository of its own and a place in the Marketplace.

docs.title: UniFi
docs.text:
Clients go into Discovery with address, MAC and name; UniFi devices (switches, access points, gateways) that are hosts report online or offline. Read-only. Sign in with:

Setup Choose You need UniFi OS Server (self-hosted), or a console (UDM, UCG, Cloud Key) Local account — UniFi OS Server or console the URL (https://host:11443 for UniFi OS Server, port 443 on a console), a local account The Network application installed on its own Local account — Network application the URL with port 8443, a local account A console with Network 9.3 or newer API key Network → Settings → Control Plane → Integrations Anything adopted in unifi.ui.com Site Manager API key unifi.ui.com → API → Create API key

The form only shows what the chosen sign-in needs.

The account. Make one for labdex: Admins & Users → add an admin, Restrict to local access only, role View Only for Network. Accounts with two-factor sign-in (UI.com accounts usually) can't be used; labdex says so. labdex signs out after each run.

Site Manager. labdex lists the consoles the key sees (or the ones named under Consoles) and reads each through the UniFi cloud connector, which needs a recent console firmware. A console the connector can't reach still reports its devices from Site Manager, without clients; the job log says which. The certificate of api.ui.com is always checked.

Cables. Signed in with a local account, Read devices also reads which port everything sits on: each switch's LLDP neighbours, each device's uplink, and the switch port of every wired client. They show up as suggestions under Inventory › Cables › Seen by switches. A wired client has no port name of its own; its interface with that MAC is used (and named eth0 if it has no name yet). The API key sign-ins don't tell ports.

TLS. UniFi uses a self-signed certificate. Either leave Check the TLS certificate off, or install a real certificate (or set a CA file) and turn it on.

docs.title: SNMP neighbours
docs.text:
Reads switches and routers over SNMP, v2c (a community) or v3 (a user with SHA, SHA-256, SHA-512 or MD5 authentication and AES-128 privacy): who sits on which port, from LLDP and, on Cisco gear, CDP. What it finds becomes suggested cables under Inventory › Cables › Seen by switches; it also reports whether each switch answers, and a host's Dashboard shows its neighbours.

It starts with the hosts tagged snmp; change Applies to for more. A host is asked at its primary address, or at the one its Address for SNMP says. Neighbours are matched to hosts by the name they announce (any name labdex knows, with or without the domain), the chassis MAC (an interface MAC in the inventory) or the management address. Ones labdex doesn't know are listed too, with a button to add them as hosts.

Give the community or the v3 passphrases from the vault to share them between instances. SNMPv3 passphrases need eight characters at least. Read-only: labdex never sets anything.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: OPNsense with FRR (its diagnostics API) or Cisco IOS-XE (RESTCONF). Lists BGP neighbours (matched to hosts), routed prefixes that aren't an inventory network, and inventory networks the router has no route for. A neighbour leaving Established notifies.

docs.title: Traefik
docs.text: Read-only, Traefik v2 or v3 API (api.insecure, or behind a router with basic auth). Import services from routers plans a service per HTTP router with a Host rule: on the host its backend points at, or, when the backend isn't in the inventory (a container address), on the Traefik host with port 443/80. The router's host name becomes the service's DNS name (grafana.example.com., a full name), so the Services page links to it. A Routers page shows each router, its backend and whether the inventory has it.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Read-only Engine API, best through a socket proxy that only allows containers and the version (e.g. CONTAINERS=1). Import containers plans:

  • a host per container (srv-ct-<service>-NN, the container name as fun name), running on the Docker host, in its zone; an interface only where the container has an address in an inventory network (macvlan/ipvlan);
  • services: published ports on the Docker host (that's where they listen), Traefik router labels as services with the router's host name on the container's host.

Turn off "containers as hosts" to get only services on the Docker host. Read container state reports running / stopped as host status.

docs.title: Installing plugins and trust
docs.text:
Plugins › Marketplace installs what the official repository and your own repositories offer; Settings › Plugins uploads a .zip and manages repositories and keys. For a download, labdex unpacks the archive, validates the manifest, checks the labdex version range and the signature before any plugin code runs, then shows what you're about to install.

Trust Means built in part of labdex and only updates with it (backups, the demo lab) official maintained by the labdex project in its own repository, signed with the project key, from the official repository community signed with the key of a repository you added, or an author key you trust unsigned no signature: installs only after you tick "I trust its author" invalid bad signature, unknown key or files changed after signing: never loaded

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
A repository is a signed index.json next to the plugin archives, on any web server. Its key signs the index and every plugin in it. When you add one, labdex shows its name and key id: compare it with the one the publisher gives you. The key is pinned from then on; a re-signed index or a plugin signed with another key is refused.

The official Marketplace (labdex-plugins, https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex-plugins/index.json) is trusted out of the box. Every official plugin lives in its own git repository; its signed releases are the versions you can install.

Since 1.24.1 no plugin ships with labdex: the official ones (OPNsense, Technitium, Proxmox, Ansible, …) are installed from the Marketplace like any other, downloaded and signature-checked. A fix for one arrives through the official repository without waiting for a labdex release. Backups and the demo lab are part of labdex itself (built in). A broken update never replaces a working copy.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
A plugin names the labdex versions it works with (labdex: ">=1.0,<2"). labdex refuses to install one outside its range, doesn't load an installed one that falls outside after an upgrade, and the Marketplace marks it as needing another labdex.

A plugin's details in the Marketplace show what's new since the version you have, and every version its repository offers, with its notes: install any of them, newer or older (each goes through the same signature check). Updates go to the newest version that isn't withdrawn and works with your labdex.

  • Switch back: after an update the version it replaced is kept, so you can go back to it in one step (and forward again the same way), even offline.
  • Stay on a version: a held plugin isn't offered updates and never updates by itself.
  • Withdrawn versions: a publisher can withdraw a version (a serious bug, say). If you have it, the Marketplace says so, with the reason, and offers a way off it; updates skip it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Settings › Plugins › Updates decides what happens when a repository has something new (labdex looks every six hours, or when you press Check now):

Setting Does Tell me (default) a notification for each new version, once (event plugins.update); nothing is installed Install official updates updates signed with the labdex project key install by themselves and land in History (plugins.updated, or plugins.update_failed); others are announced Off no checks, no notifications; the Marketplace still shows updates when you open it

An installed version that gets withdrawn is announced too (plugins.withdrawn). Route these events to ntfy, Matrix, email or a webhook under Settings › Notifications.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Official and built-in plugins run inside labdex. Community and unsigned plugins run isolated: every call (an action, a page, a widget) starts a process of its own with an empty environment, which locks itself with Linux's Landlock before the plugin is loaded. It can read Python and the plugin's own folder and write to a data folder of its own (plugin-data/<instance>) and a temporary folder; nothing else. So it can't open labdex's database, secret.key, other plugins or other integrations' secrets, can't read labdex's memory and can't signal it. Its Ansible playbooks run inside the same lock, and secrets from the vault ({$secret: …}) aren't filled in for it.

What it gets is the plugin API: the inventory, its own instance's settings and host settings, state, host status, notifications, discovery records. It can still reach the network, so treat what the inventory holds as visible to it.

The Plugins page shows which plugins run isolated and whether this machine supports Landlock. Set LABDEX_PLUGIN_SANDBOX=strict to refuse isolated plugins where it doesn't, or off to run them inside labdex (as before 1.5).

Warning

Install plugins you trust. Isolation limits what a plugin can take; it doesn't make a plugin's own actions (the changes it plans) trustworthy.

docs.title: Kubernetes workloads & Flux
docs.text:
The Kubernetes workloads & Flux integration shows what runs in one cluster and whether Flux keeps it in step with git. Towards the cluster it is read-only: labdex only sends GET requests and never changes the cluster. Add one integration per cluster, in the site the cluster belongs to. Like the Pulumi plugin it lives in plugins/kubernetes/ of the labdex repository for now.

It sits next to the k3s / Kubernetes plugin, which matches nodes to inventory hosts and reports their readiness as host status. Use both on a cluster: k3s for the nodes, this one for what runs on them.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
On the integration's Cluster page:

  • Flux: every Kustomization and HelmRelease, failing ones first, with its Ready state and message, the revision it applied (main@sha1:…, or the chart version), its source and path or chart. Suspended objects are marked.
  • Sources: the GitRepositories, OCIRepositories and HelmRepositories, with URL, branch or tag and the revision they fetched.
  • Workloads: Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets with ready against wanted replicas and their images. Leave out namespaces hides system namespaces (kube-system by default).

A dashboard widget lists what isn't ready, or says that everything is.

Read workloads and Flux runs every 5 minutes by default. When a Flux object starts failing, or a workload goes from ready to fewer ready replicas than wanted, it sends a notification: plugin.kubernetes.flux.failed or plugin.kubernetes.workload.degraded. Pick them for a channel in Settings › Notifications. The first read after adding the integration only learns the current state.

A cluster without Flux still shows its workloads.

docs.title: A read-only token
docs.text:
Create a service account that may only read what the plugin asks for, and give labdex its token:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: labdex, namespace: kube-system}
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata: {name: labdex-read}
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [nodes, pods]
    verbs: [get, list]
  - apiGroups: [apps]
    resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
    verbs: [get, list]
  - apiGroups: [kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io, helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io, source.toolkit.fluxcd.io]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: [get, list]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata: {name: labdex-read}
roleRef: {apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: ClusterRole, name: labdex-read}
subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: labdex, namespace: kube-system}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: labdex-token
  namespace: kube-system
  annotations: {kubernetes.io/service-account.name: labdex}
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token

kubectl -n kube-system get secret labdex-token -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d prints the token. The same token works for the k3s plugin. If the token can't read Flux, the page says so and shows the workloads.

Setting API server https://<address>:6443 Bearer token the service account token Cluster CA certificate-authority-data from the kubeconfig, decoded Cluster name shown on the page and in notifications Leave out namespaces space separated, default kube-system kube-public kube-node-lease

docs.title: Flux files as code
docs.text: The same integration can keep a cluster's apps as Flux files in your Flux git repository. You list the apps in labdex; labdex writes them as Flux manifests into one folder of the repository and proposes the change as a merge request. It never pushes to the branch Flux reads: Flux applies the apps when someone merges the request.

docs.title: The apps
docs.text:
Settings › Flux files › Apps is a YAML list. A Helm chart:

- name: grafana
  namespace: monitoring          # where it's installed (default: the name)
  helm: {repo: https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts, chart: grafana, version: "8.x"}
  values: {adminUser: admin}
  depends_on: [infra]

or a folder of the Flux repository, applied as a Flux Kustomization:

- name: infra
  path: ./apps/infra
  source: flux-system           # the GitRepository (default flux-system)
  prune: true

Both take interval (default 10m) and depends_on (other apps). A chart can come from an oci:// registry too. Show Flux files prints what the apps become, without touching git.

Each app becomes one file in Folder for labdex's files (default clusters/<cluster>/labdex): a HelmRepository and a HelmRelease, or a Kustomization, all in the Flux namespace. A kustomization.yaml lists them, so the folder can be included from one of your Flux Kustomizations (for example by adding it to clusters/<cluster>/kustomization.yaml). Every file starts with # Managed by labdex. labdex only ever changes or removes files that start that way; a file of the same name written by someone else stops the plan.

docs.title: Proposing the files
docs.text:
Propose Flux files is a plan:

  1. Plan: labdex fetches the Flux branch, compares labdex's folder with the apps and lists every file it would create, change or remove, with the diff. Nothing is written.
  2. Approve: every run waits for a person's approval, whatever the approval policy says.
  3. Apply: labdex commits the files on top of the branch it planned against, pushes the commit to its own branch labdex/flux-<cluster> and opens a merge request (GitLab) or pull request (GitHub) into the Flux branch. If the Flux branch moved since the plan, it stops and asks for a new plan.

It needs the repository's https address (or a local path), the branch Flux reads, and a token that may push branches and open merge requests (GitLab: a project access token with api and write_repository; GitHub: a fine-grained token with Contents and Pull requests).

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus
docs.text: Reads up from a VictoriaMetrics or Prometheus API: a host is down when every target that belongs to it is down. CPU and memory widgets on host pages.

docs.title: Beszel
docs.text: Host status, CPU, memory and disk from Beszel agents. Adds hosts as systems (plan/apply) and installs the agent over Ansible.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text: Plans a monitor per service that has a link and reads host and service status back. Needs the uptimekuma extra (in the image).

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
Checks the TLS certificate of every https service (and endpoints you list): days left, issuer, names; warns before expiry and notifies.

Status from any of these shows as live dots on Hosts and in the sidebar, on the Services page, and as host.down / host.up notifications.

docs.title: OPNsense
docs.text:
Checked against OPNsense 26.1. Give labdex its own API user with access to the pages for the actions you use: aliases, automation filter rules, destination NAT, Kea DHCP, interfaces and diagnostics (ARP).

Action Mode Check connection run Sync aliases plan generated and custom aliases, category automation:labdex; adds hosts to aliases you made by hand and only removes what it added Sync policy rules plan rules from the zone matrix and services' allow from Sync port forwards plan destination NAT for public services Sync DHCP reservations plan Kea DHCPv4 reservations from MAC/IP pairs Check access run every service's allow from against the pass rules Import ARP / leases run into Discovery

Pages: Firewall access (the access check for every host). How the firewall matches the zone matrix (pending rule changes, rules no policy explains, zones managed by labdex) is on Network › Policy › On the firewalls. On a host: the rules that mention it and its access check.

Settings worth knowing: wan_interface and nat_destination for port forwards.

Everything labdex writes carries the category automation:labdex and a key in the description; it never changes anything else.

docs.title: Patching (Ansible)
docs.text:
The Patching integration installs the waiting updates on the hosts of a site with Ansible, reboots where one is needed if you allow it, and reports every host's state back to the Patches page. Nothing reaches a host before a person approved the run.

Add it under Plugins › Patching (Ansible) › Add, in the site it should patch. Like the Pulumi plugin it lives in plugins/patching/ of the labdex repository for now.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• Ansible in labdex: build the image with docker build --build-arg ANSIBLE=1 .. Check setup says what's missing.
  • SSH to the hosts: an SSH user and private key (share one key with the Ansible runner by picking the same global secret), and sudo for that user.
  • Python 3 on the hosts, which Debian, Ubuntu, Proxmox VE and RHEL-like systems have.

docs.title: Install updates
docs.text:
Install updates is a plan:

  1. Plan. Each host the integration applies to that has updates waiting, according to its last patch report, gets a line: how many updates, how many of them security updates, and what happens about a reboot. Planning doesn't connect to any host. Hosts without a recent report are left out (so switches and appliances are never touched) unless you name them or turn on Patch hosts without a report.
  2. Approve. Every run waits for a person's approval, even when an approval policy would let it apply by itself. A policy can ask for more (two approvals, certain approvers, a change window), not for less.
  3. Apply. One play, one host at a time by default (Hosts at a time). It upgrades with the host's package manager (apt dist-upgrade, dnf/yum upgrade), checks whether a reboot is needed (/var/run/reboot-required, needs-restarting -r), reboots if allowed, and runs labdex-patch-report on the host to report back. The run stops at the first host that fails; the hosts after it stay as they were. Whatever was reported before the failure still counts.
Parameter Only these hosts host names; empty = every host the integration applies to Reboot never or if_needed; empty = the integration's setting Only hosts with security updates leave out hosts that only have other updates

docs.title: Reboots
docs.text:
Reboot is never by default. With if_needed, a host is rebooted after patching when it asks for it, except:

  • a host that runs guests in the inventory (a Proxmox node with VMs, a Docker host), unless Reboot hosts that run guests is on;
  • a host whose Never reboot this host setting is on.

The plan says for each host whether it would be rebooted and why not.

docs.title: Kubernetes nodes
docs.text:
When some of the hosts are nodes of a Kubernetes cluster, fill in Kubernetes nodes in the settings (API server, a bearer token, the cluster CA). A host counts as a node when the node has its name or one of its IP addresses. Then:

  • the plan says so for each node (drained first, uncordoned once Ready); planning only reads the node list;
  • the other hosts are patched first, in one play; then the nodes, one at a time: cordon, evict its pods (DaemonSet pods, static pods and finished pods stay), patch and reboot it as above, wait until it is Ready again, uncordon;
  • a pod a PodDisruptionBudget holds back is tried again until Wait for a drain runs out. Then the run stops, and the node stays cordoned with nothing installed, so you can look at it. The same goes for a node that isn't Ready within the reboot timeout. Uncordon it yourself (kubectl uncordon <node>) once it's fine.

Give the token its own service account, with only what draining needs:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: labdex-patching
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [nodes]
    verbs: [get, list, patch]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods]
    verbs: [list]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods/eviction]
    verbs: [create]

docs.title: On a schedule
docs.text: Save Install updates as a job template, for example every Sunday at 03:00 with Reboot: if_needed. The plan is made on time and waits for an approval (the plan.waiting notification tells you); with a change window in the policy it then applies in the window, not the moment you approve.

docs.title: Read patch state
docs.text: Read patch state runs labdex-patch-report --dry-run on every host over SSH and shows the result on the Updates page, without installing anything there and without root. It's an alternative to the cron job on each host, and can run on a schedule (Schedule in the settings).

docs.title: Leaving hosts out
docs.text: Use the integration's Applies to selectors (for example zone:DC_*), or a host's Never patch this host setting.

docs.title: Pulumi (public site)
docs.text:
The Pulumi integration keeps the hosts of a site in existence at cloud providers: a Contabo instance per node and a Cloudflare A/AAAA record per name. You describe the nodes in labdex like any other host; labdex turns them into a Pulumi program, shows what pulumi preview would change as a plan, and runs pulumi up once the plan is approved.

Add it under Plugins › Pulumi (public site) › Add, and put it in the site it should manage (usually public). The engine is part of labdex (labdex.iac); the plugin itself lives in plugins/pulumi/ of the labdex repository until it gets a repository of its own and a place in the Marketplace.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• The Pulumi SDK and CLI in labdex: build the image with docker build --build-arg PULUMI=1 ., or for a checkout pip install -e "backend[pulumi]" plus the CLI from pulumi.com. Test connection says what's missing.
  • A state passphrase. Pulumi keeps its state in labdex's data folder (pulumi/<integration>/), one stack per integration named after its site, with its secrets encrypted under this passphrase. No Pulumi Cloud account is involved. Backups carry the stacks as pulumi-state.tar.gz; to restore them, unpack that file into the data folder (tar -xzf pulumi-state.tar.gz -C /data).
  • For Contabo: an API client (client ID and secret) and API user (e-mail and password) from the Customer Control Panel › API.
  • For Cloudflare: an API token limited to Zone › DNS › Edit on one zone, the zone's name and its ID.

docs.title: What it makes
docs.text:
For every host the integration applies to (its site, its Applies to selectors and per-host switches):

Resource From Contabo instance the host's name as display name; product, region and image from the host's settings or the integration's defaults; SSH keys on new instances Cloudflare A record <record name>.<zone>, with the template {fun} (the host's first fun name, else its name) or {host}; {fun}.node gives everest.node.example.com. The address is the host's primary public IPv4, or the new instance's address while the inventory has none Cloudflare AAAA record the same, for the primary public IPv6, when AAAA records too is on

Private addresses (RFC 1918, CGNAT, ULA, link-local) never get a record. Show what Pulumi would keep lists the resources without running Pulumi.

docs.title: Existing nodes and records
docs.text:
Nothing has to be recreated. On a host's page, the Pulumi panel takes:

  • Contabo instance id: Pulumi adopts that instance (an import) instead of ordering a new one. The integration's Contabo instances page lists every instance with its id and the host it belongs to.
  • Existing A / AAAA record id: the same for Cloudflare records.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Every change is a plan first, with the usual approvals, change windows and history.
  • Instances are protected by default: a host taken out of the inventory never deletes its VPS. Turn Protect instances off to let a plan remove one, and Cancel instances removed from the inventory on to actually cancel it at Contabo; otherwise labdex only forgets it.
  • Changing an instance's product, region or image means a new instance; the plan says replaced so it can't pass unnoticed.
  • Credentials are passed to Pulumi as environment variables for the run; they're never written to the stack's state or shown in a plan.
  • Read back from the providers (pulumi refresh) updates the state from Contabo and Cloudflare, so changes made by hand show up in the next plan.

docs.title: Limits of this first version
docs.text:
• Contabo instances are a Pulumi dynamic resource (there's no Contabo package for Pulumi on PyPI): create, rename, adopt and cancel. Reinstalling, snapshots and private networks aren't managed yet.
  • Cloudflare R2 buckets, other record types and other providers (Hetzner, AWS …) would be new resource types in labdex.iac.
  • New instances' addresses are logged after an apply; add them to the host yourself.

docs.title: Technitium DNS
docs.text:
Checked against Technitium DNS Server 15.6. Use an API token limited to the zones labdex manages.

  • Sync records (plan): the inventory's records plus custom ones, into the closest zone on the server. Only records it created (marked in their comment) are changed or removed.
  • Split horizon (setting, on by default): each public service name becomes an internal zone with the service's internal addresses. The zone is created as part of the plan.
  • Per host: every record that belongs to it, flagged in sync, missing, stale or unmanaged.
  • Records pointing at addresses that aren't in the inventory go into Discovery.
